title: Network ACLs (stateless subnet boundary)
hook: A Network Access Control List (NACL) is a stateless subnet-level firewall evaluated in rule number order. Unlike security groups, NACLs support explicit deny rules — useful for blocking known bad CIDRs at the subnet edge.

blocks.text: Each subnet associates with exactly one NACL (default NACL allows all). NACL rules are numbered (e.g., 100, 200) and evaluated lowest-first until a match. Stateless means inbound and outbound are independent — allowing inbound tcp/443 requires a separate outbound rule for ephemeral return ports. NACLs filter before security groups on the way in.

entries.plainDefinition: Stateless subnet boundary firewall with numbered allow/deny rules.
Inbound and outbound rules are evaluated independently — no connection tracking.
entries.example: Must allow outbound ephemeral ports for inbound HTTP responses.

entries.plainDefinition: Lower numbers evaluate first; first match wins.
entries.example: Rule 100 deny bad IP; rule 200 allow 10.0.0.0/16.

entries.plainDefinition: Temporary client ports used for TCP/UDP return traffic — must be allowed outbound on NACL.

blocks.text: Most designs rely on security groups alone. NACLs add subnet-level guardrails: block a malicious CIDR, separate DMZ subnet policy, or compliance deny lists. Interviewers test stateless behavior — the classic 'inbound 443 allowed but responses dropped' mistake.

blocks.title: SG vs NACL
blocks.body: Security group = stateful ENI allow-only. NACL = stateless subnet allow/deny with numbered rules.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Inbound to subnet
items.body: NACL inbound rules evaluated first (lowest rule number).

items.title: Reach ENI
items.body: Security group inbound rules evaluated on the ENI — stateful.

items.title: Outbound from subnet
items.body: Security group outbound (stateful return), then NACL outbound rules separately.

items.title: Deny wins at NACL
items.body: Explicit NACL deny blocks before SG if rule matches first.

diagram.title: NACL vs security group order
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  IN[Inbound packet] --> NACL_IN[NACL inbound rules stateless]
  NACL_IN --> SG_IN[Security group inbound stateful]
  SG_IN --> ENI[ENI / instance]
  ENI --> SG_OUT[Security group outbound]
  SG_OUT --> NACL_OUT[NACL outbound rules]

snippet.label: CLI — deny known bad CIDR on NACL
snippet.code:
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry \
  --network-acl-id acl-0abc \
  --rule-number 50 \
  --protocol -1 \
  --rule-action deny \
  --egress false \
  --cidr-block 198.51.100.0/24
snippet.explanation: Low rule number ensures deny matches before broader allow rules.

snippet.label: CloudFormation — private subnet NACL
snippet.code:
PrivateNacl:
  Type: AWS::EC2::NetworkAcl
  Properties:
    VpcId: !Ref Vpc

AllowVpcInbound:
  Type: AWS::EC2::NetworkAclEntry
  Properties:
    NetworkAclId: !Ref PrivateNacl
    RuleNumber: 100
    Protocol: -1
    RuleAction: allow
    Egress: false
    CidrBlock: 10.0.0.0/16
snippet.explanation: Custom NACL replaces default allow-all when you need explicit subnet policy.

snippet.label: CLI — allow ephemeral return traffic
snippet.code:
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry \
  --network-acl-id acl-0abc \
  --rule-number 120 \
  --protocol 6 \
  --port-range From=1024,To=65535 \
  --rule-action allow \
  --egress true \
  --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0
snippet.explanation: Stateless NACL needs outbound ephemeral allow for TCP responses to inbound connections.

snippet.label: CLI — associate NACL with subnet
snippet.explanation: Each subnet has one NACL association — changing it affects all ENIs in the subnet.

blocks.title: Defense layers
rows: IP block lists in middleware — rare at L7

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Allow inbound 443 without outbound ephemeral range — responses die at NACL. Rule 100 allow all before rule 50 deny — ordering wrong. Replacing default NACL without documenting ephemeral rules.

blocks.text: Default NACL allows all — custom NACLs start implicit deny at end. NACL changes apply instantly to all subnet ENIs. How to prove it in production: Flow Logs show REJECT with NACL action; temporarily open ephemeral outbound rule and watch SYN-ACK succeed; Reachability Analyzer includes NACL in path.

rows: Drift if one AZ edited manually

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying NACLs are stateful like security groups. Strong answer: stateless numbered rules with explicit deny; must mirror inbound/outbound for TCP flows.

interviewTakeaways: NACLs are stateless subnet firewalls with numbered allow and deny rules.
Evaluated lowest rule number first; separate inbound and outbound rule sets.
Allow inbound 443 requires outbound ephemeral port rule — unlike stateful SG.
60s: Subnet boundary, stateless, deny supported, rule order matters. SG is stateful ENI layer inside. Use NACL for CIDR block lists.
Follow-up: what ephemeral port range would you allow for HTTPS responses?
commonPitfalls: Calling NACLs stateful — rejected; that is security groups.
Strong answer: stateless, numbered rules, explicit deny, need return path rules.
Inbound allow without outbound ephemeral — classic silent TCP hang.
Rule ordering wrong — broad allow at 100 prevents deny at 200 from ever matching.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Express rate-limit by IP runs at L7 after packets already passed NACL/SG — NACL deny is earlier and cheaper for known bad CIDRs.
Public ALB subnets may use different NACL than private app subnets — TypeScript deploy targets must land in subnets whose NACL permits ALB health paths.
